recent_candidates.title: This Wednesday: Daniel Mendelsohn on Dante, Petrarch, Shakespeare, and Goethe
recent_candidates.excerpt: The Boys’ Stories: Daniel Mendelsohn on Dante, Petrarch, Shakespeare, and Goethe The second seminar in our “Unrequited Love” series spans the late Middle Ages to the early Romantic era, focusing on works in which male narrators’ furious—and unreciprocated—passions lead them to acts of creation or destruction. Dante’s La Vita Nuova tracks how his childhood obsession with Bice di Portinari (“Beatrice” in his later poems) turned him into a poet. Petrarch, taking a leaf from the Roman poets, solidified many of the tropes of the genre for centuries to come in his Canzoniere, which charts the course of his hopeless idolization of “Laura” both during and after her lifetime. Side-by-side with Petrarch we will read some of Shakespeare’s “Dark Lady” sonnets. This seminar concludes with two sessions devoted to Goethe’s The Sorrows of Young Werther, a semiautobiographical epistolary novel whose anguished representation of unrequited loves resulting in self-destruction heralded the coming of the Romantic movement (and unleashed a spate of “copycat suicides” among young fans).
